steps.prompt: How many degrees do the angles of a pentagon add up to? Can you split it into triangles to find out?

cards.title: Angle sums
cards.body: Diagonals from one corner split an $n$-gon into $n - 2$ triangles, so its interior angles add to $180(n - 2)$. In a regular $n$-gon each interior angle is $\frac{180(n - 2)}{n}$. The exterior angles of any convex polygon add to $360^\circ$, so a regular one has exterior angles of $\frac{360}{n}$.

cards.title: Worked example: a regular octagon
cards.problem: What is each interior angle of a regular octagon?

try.prompt: What is the angle sum, in degrees?

cards.title: Diagonals and hexagons
cards.body: An $n$-gon has $\frac{n(n - 3)}{2}$ diagonals. A regular hexagon is six equilateral triangles, so with side $s$ its area is $\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2$ and its long diagonal is $2s$.

cards.title: Worked example: sides from an angle
cards.problem: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is $150^\circ$. How many sides does it have?

steps.text: The exterior angles add to $360$, so there are $\frac{360}{30} = 12$ sides.

cards.title: The common trap: n instead of n − 2
cards.body: The angle sum is $180(n - 2)$, not $180n$. The exterior angles always add to $360^\circ$, whatever $n$ is. Working with exterior angles is usually the fastest route to $n$.

prompts: Why do exterior angles make regular-polygon problems faster?
